summary.text: Choose a slowly divergent budget as the inverse of rapidly growing bounds \(C(t)=2L(t)^t\); if no parity support of fewer than \(t\) edges controls all closed walks of length at most \(L(t)\), branching on violated walks produces a subgraph of at most \(C(t)\) vertices for which every 2-cut has at least \(t\) monochromatic edges, contradicting the deletion budget. Minimum supports and buffered recolorings then inductively produce an independent odd-cycle transversal in every finite subgraph, making it 3-colorable; compactness yields a 3-coloring of the whole graph, contradicting infinite chromatic number.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the statement by constructing one particular function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), tending to infinity extremely slowly, for which every graph satisfying the asserted local edge-deletion bounds is in fact 3-colorable.

Throughout, graphs are simple. For a Boolean assignment \(p:V(G)\to\{0,1\}\), call an edge \(uv\) bad if \(p(u)=p(v)\), and write
\[
 F_G(p)=\{uv\in E(G):p(u)=p(v)\}.
\]
Thus \(p\) is a proper 2-coloring after all the edges in \(F_G(p)\) are removed.

We shall use the following rapidly growing numerical functions. Define \(R,L,C:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) by
\[
 R(0)=0,
\]
\[
 L(t)=16t\bigl(R(t-1)+2\bigr),
\]
and, equivalently for \(t\geq 1\),
\[
 R(t)=tL(t)+R(t-1)+3.
\]
Finally put
\[
 C(t)=2L(t)^t.
\]
(The value \(L(0)=0\), so \(C(0)=2\).) These functions are nondecreasing. Indeed, \(R\) is plainly nondecreasing from its recurrence, and then the formula for \(L\) shows that \(L\) is nondecreasing. It follows that \(C\) is nondecreasing as well; the case involving \(C(0)=2\) is immediate, and for positive indices both the base and exponent increase. We also have
\[
 t\leq L(t)\leq C(t)
\]
for positive \(t\), and hence \(t\leq C(t)\) for every \(t\).

Define
\[
 f(n)=\min\{k:n\leq C(k+1)\}.
\]
The set in this definition is nonempty, since \(n\leq C(n+1)\). Monotonicity of \(C\) gives the useful equivalence
\[
 f(n)\leq k\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\leq C(k+1).                 \tag{1}
\]
In particular, whenever \(t>0\) and \(n\leq C(t)\),
\[
 f(n)<t.                                                               \tag{2}
\]
Also \(f(n)\to\infty\). To see this, fix \(t\). If \(n>C(t)\) and one had \(f(n)<t\), then \(f(n)+1\leq t\), and the definition of \(f\), followed by monotonicity of \(C\), would give
\[
 n\leq C(f(n)+1)\leq C(t),
\]
a contradiction. Thus all \(n>C(t)\) satisfy \(f(n)\geq t\).

The main part of the argument is the following finite theorem.

**Finite theorem.** Let \(G\) be a finite graph with the following hereditary small-cut property:

for every integer \(k\geq2\), and every subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) having at most \(C(k)\) vertices, there is a Boolean assignment on the ambient vertex set for which \(H\) has fewer than \(k\) bad edges.                                      \(\tag{SC}\)

Then \(G\) is 3-colorable.

We prove this theorem in several steps.

### 1. Short parity supports

For a finite edge set \(S\subseteq E(G)\), label every unordered pair of vertices by
\[
 a_S(e)=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&e\in S,\\
 1,&e\notin S.
 \end{cases}
\]
For a walk \(W\), let \(a_S(W)\) be the sum modulo 2 of these labels over all edge occurrences of \(W\), with multiplicity. We call \(S\) an \(L\)-short support if

1. \(S\subseteq E(G)\), and
2. \(a_S(W)=0\) for every closed walk \(W\) of length at most \(L\).

Every actual bad-edge set \(F_G(p)\) is an \(L\)-short support, for every \(L\). Indeed, on an edge \(uv\),
\[
 a_{F_G(p)}(uv)=p(u)+p(v)\pmod 2:
\]
the label is 0 exactly when the endpoints have equal values. Along a walk these endpoint differences telescope, and on a closed walk their sum is 0.

Because the graph is finite, an \(L\)-short support of minimum cardinality exists. If \(S\) is such a minimum support, then
\[
 |S|\leq |F_G(p)|                                                   \tag{3}
\]
for every Boolean assignment \(p\).

We next show that property \((SC)\) produces a small short support.

**Certificate lemma.** Let \(L\geq2\) and \(t\in\mathbb N\). If there is no \(L\)-short support with fewer than \(t\) edges, then there is a subgraph \(H\subseteq G\), on at most
\[
 2L^t
\]
vertices, such that every Boolean assignment has at least \(t\) bad edges in \(H\).

Here is the full finite search proving the lemma. At a search node record a set \(D\subseteq E(G)\) of already selected, distinct edges, with \(|D|<t\). Since \(D\) is not an \(L\)-short support, some closed walk \(W\), of length at most \(L\), has \(a_D(W)=1\). For any Boolean assignment under which all edges of \(D\) are bad, the bad-edge set itself has parity zero on \(W\). Consequently at least one occurrence in \(W\) is an edge which is bad but not in \(D\). We branch over all distinct edges of \(W\setminus D\), adding one of them to \(D\). There are at most \(L\) branches.

After \(t-|D|\) levels, \(D\) has size \(t\), so any assignment making all of \(D\) bad already has at least \(t\) bad edges. Take the union of the closed walks appearing in this finite search tree. More formally, if \(s_L(n)\) is the maximum number of vertices needed below a node with \(n\) levels remaining, then
\[
 s_L(0)=0,\qquad s_L(n+1)\leq L+L s_L(n).                            \tag{4}
\]
A nonempty closed walk of length at most \(L\) has at most \(L\) distinct vertices, because its initial vertex is repeated at the end. By induction from (4), for \(L\geq2\),
\[
 s_L(n)+2\leq 2L^n.
\]
In particular the union at the root has at most \(2L^t\) vertices.

To verify its asserted property, take any Boolean assignment. Starting at the root, as long as all currently selected edges are bad, the parity argument above supplies a bad edge on the node's closed walk outside the current set, and we follow the branch corresponding to that edge. At depth \(t\), all \(t\) selected edges are bad. Thus the assignment has at least \(t\) bad edges in the union subgraph. This proves the certificate lemma.

Apply the contrapositive under \((SC)\). For \(t\geq2\), choose \(L=L(t)\). We have \(L(t)\geq2\), and
\[
 2L(t)^t=C(t).
\]
If no \(L(t)\)-short support had fewer than \(t\) edges, the certificate lemma would give a subgraph on at most \(C(t)\) vertices in which every cut has at least \(t\) bad edges, contradicting \((SC)\). Hence
\[
 \text{there is an \(L(t)\)-short support \(T\) with \(|T|<t\).}     \tag{5}
\]
In particular, a minimum \(L(t)\)-short support \(S\) also satisfies \(|S|<t\).

### 2. Locality of a minimum support

For an edge set \(A\), let \(\partial A\) denote the set of all endpoints of edges in \(A\). Say a vertex is within radius \(r\) of a set \(X\) if there is an actual graph walk of length at most \(r\) from that vertex to a member of \(X\). This definition also behaves correctly in disconnected graphs.

**Locality lemma.** If \(S\) is a minimum \(L\)-short support and \(F\) is any other \(L\)-short support, every vertex of \(\partial S\) is within distance \(|S|L\) of \(\partial F\).

We prove this by flooding the edges of \(S\), one at a time. Suppose \(D\subseteq S\), \(|D|<|S|\), and every endpoint of \(D\) is within radius \(r\) of \(\partial F\). Since \(S\) is minimum, \(D\) cannot itself be an \(L\)-short support. Thus there is a closed walk \(W\), of length at most \(L\), with \(a_D(W)=1\). Since \(a_S(W)=0\), some edge
\[
 e\in S\setminus D
\]
occurs on \(W\). Since also \(a_F(W)=0\), comparison of \(a_D\) and \(a_F\) shows that some edge \(g\) occurring on \(W\) belongs to \(D\cup F\). Any two vertices occurring on a walk can be joined, possibly by reversing the appropriate segment, by a walk no longer than the original walk. Hence every endpoint of \(e\) is within \(L\) of an endpoint of \(g\). If \(g\in D\), that endpoint is already within radius \(r\) of \(\partial F\); if \(g\in F\), it is itself in \(\partial F\). Thus every endpoint of \(e\) is within radius \(r+L\) of \(\partial F\).

Starting with \(D=\varnothing\), repeat this step \(|S|\) times. We obtain all of \(S\), and its endpoints lie within radius \(|S|L\) of \(\partial F\), proving the lemma. Taking \(F=F_G(p)\), which is a short support by telescoping, gives
\[
 \partial S\subseteq N_{|S|L}\bigl(\partial F_G(p)\bigr).           \tag{6}
\]

### 3. Potentials on finitely many terminals

We need a simultaneous parity-potential lemma.

**Potential lemma.** Let \(a:E(G)\to\{0,1\}\) be an edge label, let \(W\) be a finite set of terminals, and let \(D\geq0\). Suppose every closed walk of length at most \(2|W|D\) has \(a\)-sum zero. Then there is a Boolean function \(q\) on the vertices such that, whenever \(u,v\in W\) and \(P\) is a walk from \(u\) to \(v\) of length at most \(D\),
\[
 a(P)=q(u)+q(v)\pmod2.                                               \tag{7}
\]

To prove this, form a double cover whose vertices are pairs \((w,b)\), with \(w\in W\) and \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Join two distinct pairs \((u,b)\), \((v,c)\) when there is a walk from \(u\) to \(v\) of length at most \(D\) and with label sum \(b+c\). A walk of \(m\) edges in this cover expands by concatenation to a walk in \(G\) of length at most \(mD\), with label sum equal to the sum of the Boolean coordinates at its endpoints.

For each \(w\), the two lifts \((w,0)\) and \((w,1)\) lie in different connected components. Otherwise take a simple path between them in the cover. The cover has \(2|W|\) vertices, so this path has length at most \(2|W|\). Its expansion is a closed walk in \(G\) of length at most \(2|W|D\) and label sum 1, contrary to the hypothesis.

Order the connected components of the cover arbitrarily, and define \(q(w)=1\) precisely when the component of \((w,0)\) precedes that of \((w,1)\). A constraint-walk of parity 0 identifies the 0-components of its endpoints and also the 1-components; a constraint-walk of parity 1 crosses these two identifications. In the first case the two values of \(q\) agree, and in the second they differ. This is exactly (7). Extend \(q\) arbitrarily away from \(W\).

We apply this to a short support. Let \(p\) be a Boolean assignment, put \(F=F_G(p)\), and let \(S\) be an \(L\)-short support satisfying \(|S|\leq |F|\). Fix a radius \(r\), and assume
\[
 16|F|(r+2)\leq L.                                                    \tag{8}
\]
Set
\[
 U=F\cup S,\qquad W=\partial U,\qquad D=2r+4.
\]
Since an edge set has at most twice as many endpoints as edges,
\[
 |W|\leq2|U|\leq2(|F|+|S|)\leq4|F|.
\]
Therefore
\[
 2|W|D\leq 16|F|(r+2)\leq L.
\]
Use the potential lemma with the label \(a_S\). Its hypothesis follows from the short-support property of \(S\). We get an assignment \(q\) with two crucial properties.

First, for each special edge \(uv\in U\), the one-edge walk gives
\[
 a_S(uv)=q(u)+q(v).
\]
Since \(a_S(uv)=0\) exactly when \(uv\in S\),
\[
 q(u)=q(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad uv\in S.                    \tag{9}
\]
Second, suppose \(u,v\in W\) are joined by a walk of length at most \(2r+4\) avoiding all edges in \(U\). On every edge of this walk, membership in both \(F\) and \(S\) fails, so the labels \(a_S\) and \(a_F\) are both 1. The telescoping identity for \(F\), together with (7), gives
\[
 q(u)+q(v)=p(u)+p(v),
\]
or equivalently
\[
 q(u)+p(u)=q(v)+p(v).                                                 \tag{10}
\]

### 4. Buffered recoloring

We now use (9) and (10) to replace the bad-edge set \(F\) by \(S\), at the cost of removing an independent set in a controlled annulus.

Let \(P=G-U\), the graph obtained by deleting the special edges. The old assignment \(p\) is proper on \(P\), since all its bad edges belong to \(F\subseteq U\). Let
\[
 X=\{w\in W:q(w)\ne p(w)\},
\]
and let \(A_i\) be the set of vertices reachable in \(P\) from \(X\) by a walk of length at most \(i\). Define
\[
 Z=\{z:p(z)=1,\ z\in A_{r+3},\ z\notin A_{r+1}\},                 \tag{11}
\]
and define a new Boolean assignment \(p_1\) by flipping \(p\) on \(A_{r+2}\):
\[
 p_1(v)=
 \begin{cases}
 1-p(v),&v\in A_{r+2},\\
 p(v),&v\notin A_{r+2}.
 \end{cases}                                                         \tag{12}
\]

We record all properties of this construction.

A terminal \(w\in W\) with \(q(w)=p(w)\) cannot be within \(P\)-distance \(2r+4\) of \(X\). Indeed, if it were joined to \(x\in X\) by such a walk, (10) would say that \(q(x)+p(x)=q(w)+p(w)=0\), contradicting \(x\in X\). It follows that every terminal lies in exactly the phase prescribed by \(q\): terminals in \(X\) are in \(A_{r+2}\), while the other terminals are not. Hence
\[
 p_1(w)=q(w)\qquad(w\in W).                                         \tag{13}
\]

No vertex of \(Z\) lies within distance \(r+1\) in \(G\) of \(W\). To justify the passage from \(G\) to \(P\), take a shortest initial segment of a walk ending at its first vertex of \(W\). Every deleted edge has both endpoints in \(W\), so no edge before that first hit is deleted. Thus a \(G\)-walk of length at most \(r+1\) from \(z\) to \(W\) gives such a \(P\)-walk. If its endpoint terminal is in \(X\), this contradicts \(z\notin A_{r+1}\). If it is not in \(X\), concatenate the reversed walk with the path of length at most \(r+3\) from \(z\) to \(X\), which exists by (11); this puts that terminal within \(2r+4\) of \(X\), contrary to the preceding paragraph. Therefore
\[
 z\in Z\implies z\notin N_{r+1}(W).                               \tag{14}
\]
On the other hand, by definition and because \(X\subseteq W\),
\[
 z\in Z\implies z\in N_{r+3}(W).                                  \tag{15}
\]

The set \(Z\) is independent. No special edge touches \(Z\), by (14), because both endpoints of every special edge are in \(W\). Thus any edge between two vertices of \(Z\) would be an edge of \(P\); but both endpoints have old color 1 by (11), contradicting that \(p\) is proper on \(P\).

It remains to find the bad edges of \(p_1\) after deleting \(Z\). On a special edge both endpoints are terminals, so (13) and (9) say it is bad under \(p_1\) exactly when it belongs to \(S\). Both endpoints of every edge of \(S\) survive, again by (14).

On an edge of \(P\), if both endpoints are in \(A_{r+2}\), both old colors are flipped, so the edge remains proper; likewise if neither endpoint is in \(A_{r+2}\). If exactly one endpoint is in \(A_{r+2}\), adjacency implies that both endpoints lie in the annulus \(A_{r+3}\setminus A_{r+1}\). Since \(p\) is proper on \(P\), one of these two endpoints has old color 1, and by (11) that endpoint belongs to \(Z\). Thus after deleting \(Z\) there is no surviving phase-crossing edge. Consequently
\[
 F_{G-Z}(p_1)=S.                                                      \tag{16}
\]

We have proved the buffered recoloring statement: under (8), there are an independent set \(Z\) and an assignment \(p_1\) such that (14), (15), and (16) hold.

### 5. Induction producing an independent odd-cycle transversal

We prove by strong induction on \(t=|F_G(p)|\) the following localized assertion:

if \(G\) satisfies \((SC)\), then there are an independent set \(I\) and a Boolean assignment \(p'\), proper on \(G-I\), such that
\[
 I\subseteq N_{R(t)}\bigl(\partial F_G(p)\bigr).                    \tag{17}
\]

For \(t=0\), take \(I=\varnothing\) and \(p'=p\).

For \(t=1\), let the unique bad edge be \(uv\), and take \(I=\{u\}\), \(p'=p\). A singleton is independent in a simple graph. Every bad edge is the unique edge \(uv\), which is incident with \(u\), so \(p\) is proper off \(I\). Also \(u\in\partial F_G(p)\), which gives (17).

Now let \(t\geq2\), write \(F=F_G(p)\), and choose a minimum \(L(t)\)-short support \(S\). By (5),
\[
 |S|<t,                                                              \tag{18}
\]
and by (3), \(|S|\leq|F|=t\). Put \(r=R(t-1)\). The definition of \(L(t)\) says exactly
\[
 16|F|(r+2)=16t(R(t-1)+2)=L(t),
\]
so buffered recoloring applies. It gives an independent set \(Z\) and an assignment \(p_1\) such that
\[
 F_{G-Z}(p_1)=S,                                                      \tag{19}
\]
\[
 Z\cap N_{r+1}(\partial(F\cup S))=\varnothing,                       \tag{20}
\]
and
\[
 Z\subseteq N_{r+3}(\partial(F\cup S)).                             \tag{21}
\]

The hereditary small-cut property passes to subgraphs, in particular to \(G-Z\): every subgraph of \(G-Z\) is also a subgraph of \(G\), and a cut with few bad edges in the latter remains such in the former. By (18), the induction hypothesis applies to \(G-Z,p_1\). It supplies an independent set \(J\) in \(G-Z\) and an assignment \(p_2\), proper on \((G-Z)-J\), with
\[
 J\subseteq N_{R(|S|)}^{G-Z}(\partial S)
   \subseteq N_r^G(\partial S).                                     \tag{22}
\]
Here we used \(|S|<t\), monotonicity of \(R\), and enlargement from the subgraph metric to the graph metric.

The union \(I=Z\cup J\) is independent in \(G\). Each part is independent in the appropriate graph. Also no edge joins \(Z\) to \(J\): by (22), a neighbor in \(Z\) of a vertex of \(J\) would be within radius \(r+1\) of \(\partial S\subseteq\partial(F\cup S)\), contradicting (20). The assignment \(p_2\) is proper outside \(I\), since it is proper outside \(J\) in \(G-Z\).

Finally we verify localization. By the locality lemma (6),
\[
 \partial S\subseteq N_{|S|L(t)}(\partial F).
\]
Thus every point of \(\partial(F\cup S)\) lies within radius \(|S|L(t)\) of \(\partial F\). From (21), every point of \(Z\) lies within radius
\[
 r+3+|S|L(t)
\]
of \(\partial F\). The same, with an even smaller initial radius, follows for \(J\) from (22). Since \(|S|<t\),
\[
 r+3+|S|L(t)
 \leq R(t-1)+3+tL(t)
 =R(t).
\]
This proves (17), completing the induction.

Take any initial Boolean assignment, for example the constant assignment. The induction gives an independent set \(I\) such that \(G-I\) is properly 2-colored. Give every vertex of \(I\) a third color and use the two Boolean colors outside \(I\). Independence of \(I\) and properness outside it show that this is a proper 3-coloring. The finite theorem is proved.

### 6. From the deletion-distance hypothesis to small cuts

We now return to the quantities in the question. Let \(A\) be a finite subgraph of a graph \(G\). Its edge set is finite. Deleting every edge makes it bipartite, so the set of admissible deletion cardinalities in the definition of the minimum distance is nonempty. Since it is a nonempty set of natural numbers, its infimum is its least member. Thus there is an actual finite set \(E\subseteq E(A)\) such that
\[
 A-E\text{ is bipartite},\qquad |E|=\operatorname{dist}(A),          \tag{23}
\]
where \(\operatorname{dist}(A)\) denotes the stated minimum edge distance to bipartiteness.

Also a graph on \(n\) vertices has at most \(\binom n2\) edges. Therefore every distance appearing in the set whose supremum defines
\(\operatorname{maxDist}_G(n)\) is at most \(\binom n2\). The set is bounded above, and for each finite \(A\), its own distance is one of the entries at \(n=|V(A)|\). Hence
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(A)\leq \operatorname{maxDist}_G(|V(A)|).       \tag{24}
\]
This also explains why the supremum in the formal statement behaves as the required maximum for the present argument.

Suppose now that
\[
 \operatorname{maxDist}_G(n)\leq f(n)\qquad\text{for every }n.       \tag{25}
\]
Combining (23)--(25), every finite subgraph \(A\) admits a finite set \(E\) of at most \(f(|V(A)|)\) edges whose deletion makes it bipartite.

A proper 2-coloring of \(A-E\) can be extended arbitrarily to an ambient Boolean assignment. Every bad edge of \(A\) under that assignment must belong to \(E\), since every edge outside \(E\) is properly colored. Thus \(A\) has a cut with at most \(|E|\) bad edges.

The same conclusion remains valid when a finite graph is represented on a finite subset of a larger ambient vertex type: restriction to the subset does not create or identify distinct edges, because the inclusion of vertices is injective. Consequently, if \(H\) is any subgraph on \(n\leq C(k)\) vertices, where \(k\geq2\), then (2) and (25) give a Boolean cut satisfying
\[
 |F_H(p)|\leq f(n)<k.                                                \tag{26}
\]
Thus every finite subgraph of \(G\), viewed as a graph on its own finite vertex set, satisfies precisely the hereditary property \((SC)\). By the finite theorem, every finite subgraph of \(G\) is 3-colorable.

### 7. Compactness and the contradiction

We use the standard compactness theorem for graph coloring: if every finite subgraph of a graph is colorable with a fixed finite set of colors, then the whole graph is colorable with that set.

For completeness, take the compact product space \(\{1,2,3\}^{V(G)}\), with each factor discrete. For every edge \(uv\), the set of assignments satisfying \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) is closed. Any finite collection of these closed conditions involves only finitely many vertices and is simultaneously satisfiable because the corresponding finite subgraph is 3-colorable. Hence these closed sets have the finite-intersection property. Compactness of the product yields an assignment satisfying all edge conditions, namely a proper 3-coloring of \(G\).

We have therefore proved:
\[
 \bigl(\forall n,\ \operatorname{maxDist}_G(n)\leq f(n)\bigr)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 G\text{ is 3-colorable}.                                           \tag{27}
\]
But the explicitly constructed function \(f\) tends to infinity. If the conjectured universal statement were true, applying it to this \(f\) would produce a graph \(G\) of infinite chromatic number satisfying the premise of (27). Equation (27) would make \(G\) 3-colorable, so its chromatic number would be finite, contradicting that its chromatic number is infinite.

Thus the proposed statement “for every \(f(n)\to\infty\) there is such a graph of infinite chromatic number” is false.
